utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like as a preliminary matter, I'd like to put a few informal communications on the record before we start with the final arguments -- closing arguments. First, on the 17th of December of last year, the Prosecution requested an extension until the 8th of February, 2013, to file the consolidated list of protective measures which was ordered on the 7th of November, 2012. That extension was granted on the 18th of December. On the 25th of January of this year, the Chamber notified the parties through another informal communication that this deadline, as well as the deadline to file public redacted versions of confidential exhibits was further moved to the 8th of March. Second, on the 7th of December of last year, the Chamber's staff informed the parties that all references to document 1D1572.1 in its 5th of November, 2012, decision on miscellaneous rebuttal documents should be understood as a reference to 1D1572. Third, on the 11th of January, 2013, the Prosecution filed a request for guidance in relation to redacting the time trial briefs. On the 17th of January of this year, the Chamber declined to give guidance expressing its confidence that the parties are able to continue implementing the Chamber's protective measures orders without further guidance. Then we are here today to hear the closing arguments, at least the beginning of it. Times allotted was four hours for the Prosecution, two and a half hours for each Defence team, and in the second round one hour for the Prosecution and one hour for the Defence teams together. Mr. Groome, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a preliminary matter in the interest of remaining in public session as much as possible, earlier today the Prosecution filed a confidential filing with references to evidence, and I believe courtesy copies have been handed out to everyone here in the court. Secondly, Your Honour. We will be using a series of slides, and it is also possible that the Chamber wants to adjust its monitors. It will be able to view those slides for a longer period of time. They will be visible on the public projection of these proceedings. With that, Your Honours, I'll begin. Your Honours, when the Prosecution opened its case on the 9th of June, 2009, I told you that this case in its simplest terms is an examination of the conduct of two of the people with primary responsibility for organising, training, funding, equipping, and directing members of the Special Units of the Serbian DB to perpetrator grievous crimes in the name of protecting Serbs and securing for them a land free from Croats and Muslims. To establish that proposition beyond reasonable doubt, the Prosecution relied on the evidence of 97 witnesses; many the victims of terrible crimes, many former members of the special units of the Serbian DB, others were Serbs who lived where crimes occurred and came forward to provide evidence about the destruction of their mixed ethnic communities. The Prosecution tendered videos and intercepted communications by both accused and thousands of pages of documents that give insight into the daily workings of the State Security Service. A large corpus of evidence which when examined brings to the light of day the covert criminal operations by the Serbian State Security Service in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, the evidence establishing the crimes alleged in the indictment is set out in detail in the Prosecution final trial brief. For those members of the public interested in learning more about this evidence, a public version of that brief will be filed in the coming days. It is not our intention today to focus on the detail of the crimes. The fact that they occurred or even how they transpired is beyond any reasonable dispute, and in fact, in several instances the accused acknowledge some of the crimes in their briefs. Rather, we will focus our remarks today on how we have established the accused's participation in and contribution to these crimes and how that demonstrates their responsibility for them. We will depart from the structure we employed in the brief and try to assist the Chamber now by organising our remarks according to a different structure, to discuss the case from the perspective of each of the special units of the Serbian State Security Service and the crimes they participated in. Our remarks are not meant to be as comprehensive as the brief, but to usefully amplify certain aspects of it. Later this afternoon Mr. Adam Weber will provide an overview of the special units of the Serbian State Security Service and address the crimes in which the Red Berets or "the unit," participated. Crimes in the Krajina in places like Glina, when on the 26th of July, 1991, 50 of the unit's first members attacked that town and neighbouring Struga, targeting the homes, schools, and churches of its non-Serb civilian population, driving them from their homes and farms. On the 5th of August, 1991, Mr. Simatovic himself would participate in the attack on Lovinac, attacking with mortars from one side and an armoured train from the other. Later that month on the 26th, Martic delivered an ultimatum to Kijevo telling non-Serbs that co-existence was no longer possible. Martic's Police ravaged the town, ransacking and burning the homes of non-Serbs. In October 1991, Martic's police and others rounded up 53 unarmed elderly and infirm people in a local firehouse. Their names had already been placed on a list there. The following day they were slaughtered in Krecane. The project of cleansing the Krajina of non-Serbs would continue in Vukovici, Saborsko, Skabrnja, and Nadin with murders and forced removals in November of 1991. After Mr. Weber describes the unit's role in these events, he will trace their movements, the movement of the unit, into Bosnia and Herzegovina where in Bosanski Samac and Doboj they used their newly honed skills on non-Serbs there with even greater efficiency. Mr. Simatovic himself would order the Red Berets into Bosanski Samac. One unit member proudly asserted that the operation to take control of the town took little more than half an hour. After that, the more time consuming task of identifying and removing the non-Serb population took place. The Red Berets under the command of Raja Bozovic worked with local forces to conduct a vicious campaign of ethnic cleansing in Doboj. Non-Serb prisoners were kept in deplorable conditions like in Spreca and Percin's Disco, places where they were detained and tortured, all the while just outside their window the Red Berets drilled and trained. For some their torture would only end on the 12th of July when they met their death on a minefield at the edge of town. However, these were not the first crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina the accused are responsible for. Their first move into Bosnia was in Bijeljina and Zvornik along the border with Serbia. These crimes perpetrated by Arkan and his Serbian Volunteer Guard or SDG, more popularly known from his television ads as Arkan's Tigers will be the focus of Rachel Friedman's submissions today. In 1996, while running for public office, Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan make the statement that we can now see on slide 5. In both Bijeljina and Zvornik, he gave ultimatums: He would destroy the towns if they were not surrendered to him, Arkan.

utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be filing with the Registrar a copy of these slides, and I apologise for any inconvenience at the moment. Hopefully it will be sorted soon. Your Honours, here on slide 5 we can see the iconic image that first introduced the world to Arkan's Tigers. Over the course of this trial, one Defence witness would put a name to the man kicking the woman who has just been murdered, Srdjan Golubovic, also known as Max. The first place Stanisic deployed Arkan's men was to Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem where they were among the most brutal perpetrators of crimes. After Bijeljina, Arkan would move south to Zvornik in co-ordination with Simatovic and the Bosnian Serb leadership. When he arrived, it was clear to the non-Serb population that their lives were under serious threat. Arkan's Tigers would be responsible for many of the killings in Zvornik. Others were committed by paramilitary groups who were given impunity to destroy the non-Serb population of the municipality. Seselj's men were among these paramilitaries, and as Seselj has publicly stated, it was a well-organised operation, organised with the direct involvement of Mr. Simatovic. We will then ask you to turn your attention to the crimes of the Skorpions and conclude with Arkan's crimes in Sanski Most in 1995. Ms. Grace Harbour will address you on these points. The Chamber is by now very familiar with the killing of six men and boys in Trnovo, taken captive during the fall of Srebrenica and brought to Trnovo to be murdered. We will amplify our written submissions on this as well as respond to some of the arguments presented in the Defence briefs. The last crimes charged in the indictment concern Arkan's crimes in Sanski Most in 1995. On the 20th of September, 1995, the SDG forced approximately 13 detainees into a truck, drove them to the village of Trnova, unloaded them in pairs, and shot them as they stumbled into an abandoned garage. The next day the SDG crowded more than 65 Bosniaks into small buses, drove them to a place called Sasina, and murdered them in cold blood, slitting the throats of some and shooting others. Your Honours, before we lead you through the evidence setting out the contribution of each accused to these crimes, it will be helpful to spend some measure of time setting out the joint criminal enterprise underlying these crimes, and for this I would now turn the podium over to Mr. Travis Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As Mr. Groome has indicated, I will be addressing the Chamber on matters related to the joint criminal enterprise, and I have six points to address. First, I'll discuss the close relationship between the accused. Second, I'll discuss the evidence that Stanisic was an astoundingly well-informed and engaged leader. Next, I'll discuss a DB document signed by Mr. Simatovic that corroborates the Prosecution evidence regarding events in the Krajina. From there, I'll move on to the accused's involvement in the common criminal plan in early 1991, including the attack on Lovinac. Then I'll briefly discuss the co-operative relationship between public security and state security, and finally, I will discuss the irrelevance of the tensions among Milosevic, Karadzic, and Krajisnik to the accused's liability for the 1995 crimes. Moving now to my first point about the relationship between the two accused. Each of the accused has sought to distance himself from the other in his final brief, but Your Honours should not be taken in by these arguments. The relationship between the accused was a close relationship of co-operation and trust throughout the indictment period. It is the most important relationship among JCE members in this case. Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic stood side by side at key moments throughout the indictment period. In P390, which we see here on slide number 10, we see them together with Karadzic and Krajisnik. And General Milovanovic testified that this photo appears to have been taken in Serbia sometime during the war. We also see a still image from P1592, in which Stanisic and Simatovic are together in Bajina Basta in the critical period following the ABiH attack on Skelani. On slide number 11, in a still from P61, we see Stanisic and Simatovic celebrating the success of their unit together with Milosevic. We also see a still from P3043, in which the accused are together at the hostage release press conference in Bosnia. I'll also mention P391, which we'll see during Mr. Weber's presentation. In that photo, we'll see Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic together again, this time with Karadzic, Krajisnik, Martic, and Stojan Zupljanin. Your Honours, I've started with these photos and video stills because they are incontestable evidence that Your Honours can see with your own eyes. But there is a tremendous amount of witness evidence on the relationship between Stanisic and Simatovic. I don't have time to summarise all of it but I'd like to make one point. At least four witnesses describe Simatovic as Stanisic's second in command. Babic calls Simatovic Stanisic's assistant, and Sliskovic puts Mr. Simatovic directly below Mr. Stanisic in the JATD chain of command. Two other witnesses give similar evidence that is set out at rows A1 to A4 of the confidential evidence chart. The evidence of these four independent witnesses is consistent not just with each other but also with the photos and video stills I've just shown you. The only reasonable inference available to Your Honours is that the relationship between the accused was characterised by a high degree of closeness and trust. Before I move to my next point I'd also just point out to the Chamber that in the pictures we just looked at, Simatovic was almost always wearing a camouflage uniform, and he was always in the company of other JCE members. This obviously contradicts his arguments that he only did operative work and was a lowly functionary. My next point concerns Mr. Stanisic's leadership and management style. Stanisic Defence witness Corbic testified --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Stanisic Defence witness Corbic testified that Mr. Stanisic was a well informed, active, and involved leader who carefully reviewed information provided to him by subordinates and who informed himself of the work of individuals several levels below him in the hierarchy. He was not content to rely solely on reporting, but he also travelled to the field to gather information for himself. That's at transcript pages 14423 to 14426, but in fact it follows from the entirety of Mr. Corbic's testimony. Mr. Corbic limited his comments to the context in which he worked with Mr. Stanisic but General Milovanovic's evidence demonstrates that these were general leadership and management traits that Stanisic applied to all of his work, something that we can see here in slide number 14. In video Exhibit P376, Milovanovic said the following: "I was astounded by Stanisic's knowledge about our situation in Podrinje. Some things he knew even better than I did. He knew who was fighting in which village, who was in command. I really was a bit amazed." In court before Your Honours, General Milovanovic confirmed that he was "quite amazed with the extent of Stanisic's knowledge and information about particular areas in Bosnia." That's at transcript page 4385. The picture that these two witnesses, Corbic and Milovanovic, paint as Stanisic's active, involved leadership and detailed knowledge of events in the field corroborates Prosecution witnesses heard throughout the case. One particular point I would like to emphasise, given that Stanisic was better informed about some aspects of VRS operations in Eastern Bosnia than General Milovanovic a senior VRS officer was. Your Honours can have no doubt that Stanisic was intimately familiar with all aspects of the operation of his own organisation. In that context, I would like to turn to P3251, a document that was obtained and uploaded by the Stanisic Defence. The Prosecution was not aware of this document until it was disclosed on e-court. This document provides powerful corroboration for the Prosecution witnesses who testified about events in the Krajina. The document which you see on slide 16 before you is an official note regarding contact with Daniel Snedden who, as Your Honours are aware, was also known as Captain Dragan. It is dated 13 April 1991, and it is signed by operative Franko Simatovic, and I note in passing that the signature on this document appears consistent with the signatures on P3039, several of which were identified by Krsmanovic as the signatures of Simatovic. The first sentence of this document is the most important, and it reads as follows: "On 13 April 1991, a meeting was held with Daniel Snedden in order to discuss the possibilities of his further engagement pursuant to the plan which was presented to him during the last meeting." This document thus speaks of at least two meetings between Daniel Snedden and the DB, at least one of which was with Simatovic. It also explicitly states that the DB is considering further, and I emphasise "further," engaging Captain Dragan. The Simatovic Defence devote 19 pages, more than 60 paragraphs, of their brief to analysing the DB monitoring of Captain Dragan, but they fail to mention this document even once. At paragraph 295, they come to the conclusion that: "The foregoing evidence shows clearly and beyond doubt that Daniel Snedden, aka Captain Dragan, had no contacts or connections with the Serbian DB." Your Honours, this single document undermines that conclusion and the analysis it relies on. It does more than that, though. It also strongly corroborates the account Captain Dragan gives in Exhibit P2976 of his contacts with Simatovic before his deployment to Knin. More generally it corroborates Captain Dragan's entire account of his co-operation with the DB. Let's listen to what Captain Dragan says about the meeting Simatovic described in P3251.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: P3251 provides strong corroboration for Captain Dragan's account, but it does more than that. It also corroborates all the other testimonial and documentary evidence that Your Honours have seen and heard through this case clearly establishing the relationship between the DB and Captain Dragan. To use just one simple example, the warm embraces between the accused and Captain Dragan at the end of the Kula video make no sense whatsoever in the context of the Defence narrative, but they are the most natural thing in the world in light of the Prosecution evidence regarding the close relationship between the accused and Captain Dragan. The Defence have aggressively challenged the credibility of Prosecution witnesses who say that Captain Dragan was engaged by the accused and that he was close to them. These witnesses are, of course, well corroborated by each other and by a large body of other evidence, but this one document signed by Simatovic and this one video, P61, show on their own that the Prosecution witnesses spoke the truth. In short, Your Honours, in light of the strong corroboration among all of the evidence, the Chamber can have no reasonable doubt that the accused sent Captain Dragan to the Krajina and that they co-operated with him while he was there. P3251, Simatovic's note about his meeting with Dragan, also refutes another argument that the Defence have made with respect to several key individuals in this case; namely that the DB could not possibly be co-operating with anyone that it was also monitoring. They have attempted this argument -- excuse me. They have attempted this argument with at least three individuals, Captain Dragan, Arkan, and Slobodan Miljkovic, aka Lugar. This argument is unpersuasive even in theory since there is nothing that would prevent the DB from working with someone they were monitoring and nothing that would prevent them from monitoring someone they were working with. But the example of Captain Dragan takes this argument from weak to entirely untenable. Given the clear evidence that the DB was indeed co-operating with Captain Dragan even as it monitored him the Chamber can draw no inferences from the evidence that the DB monitored Arkan and Lugar as well. I would now like to move to my next point regarding the existence of the common criminal plan. The Simatovic Defence argues that we have failed to prove the existence after common criminal plan design or purpose at all, while the Stanisic Defence asserts that we have failed to establish the existence of a common criminal plan prior to September 1991. With respect to the Simatovic claim that the JCE never existed at all I refer Your Honours to our submissions at the 98 bis stage which were made in response to an identical challenge by the Simatovic defence at that point in time. Regarding the Stanisic Defence claim that no criminal plan existed before September 1991, I will turn once again to Captain Dragan. The document on slide 20 before you is a Defence exhibit, a report from the 2nd administration of the Belgrade DB centre. It is dated 3 April 1991, just ten days before Simatovic's report recording his meeting with Captain Dragan. This report shows that the DB knew that Captain Dragan was potentially dangerous. It states that Snedden is inclined to terrorism, that he wished to procure a large quantity of weapons, and most importantly, that he had undertaken actions to create and arm paramilitary formations in the Knin Krajina as you see on the slide before you. In other words, the accused knew at the time they brought him to the Krajina that Captain Dragan was an aggressive and dangerous individual. This shows that the Golubic camp was not a defensive project as the Stanisic Defence has claimed. It also shows that even in April 1991, the accused intended to further the common criminal plan. The attack on the Croat village of Lovinac provides further evidence that the accused intended to further the common criminal plan in the summer of 1991. A witness described the purpose of the attack on Lovinac this way: "The target was to cleanse the village and to get the entire population out and to establish a purely Serb territory." And Your Honours have that citation on slide 21 before you now. This is precisely a statement of the common criminal plan to forcibly and permanently remove non-Serbs. Babic also confirmed that the civilian population was a target of this attack. He said that the attack was directed against the village itself as well as against the police station and that Simatovic bragged that the whole village had been destroyed. That's P1877 at page 44. At rows A5 to A9 of the confidential evidence table, Your Honours will find more evidence that this was an attack aimed at forcible displacement. Your Honours, as discussed at paragraphs 402 to 405 of our final brief, Mr. Simatovic personally participated in the attack on Lovinac together with Milan Martic. As you see on the slide before you, Babic said: "Frenki, or Franjo Simatovic ... and Milan Martic with mortars, with a mortar unit, they were the first to open fire on the village of Lovinac and thus expel the Croats from the Gracac area." Another witness also corroborates Simatovic's participation in the attack as set out at rows A10 and A11 of the confidential evidence table. And both of those witnesses are corroborated by a key document that we will now look at. A distinctive feature of the attack on Lovinac was its use of an armoured train, as set out in the confidential evidence table at rows A12 to A16. On slide number 22, we see a document that links Mr. Simatovic to this train and both Simatovic and the train to the attack on Lovinac. This document, which is signed by Mr. Simatovic, concerns the creation of an armoured train that would "have the capability to target and attack Lovinac." And the document is dated 21 June 1991. And I would draw the Chamber's attention to the initials at the bottom of the slide before we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we move on now to slide number 23. On this slide Your Honours see the initials we have just looked at from slide P2673, the armoured train document, as well as initials from Exhibits D1117, P2420, and P352. The initials on those three exhibits were identified as the initials of Mr. Simatovic by Defence witness Radivoje Micic, and the initials on all four documents appear to be consistent. Your Honours, this document, together with the consistent witness evidence regarding this attack, shows beyond reasonable doubt that the attack happened, that Simatovic participated in it, and that its purpose was to drive out the Croat civilian population. In other words, that its purpose was to further the common criminal plan. The attack also shows that the purpose of the Golubic training camp was not defensive as the Stanisic Defence have claimed. Row A15 of the confidential evidence table establishes that the crew of the armoured train was trained at Golubic. Their use in this attack shows that the purpose of training at Golubic was fundamentally linked to the common criminal plan. The attack on Ljubovo also shows that Golubic was not a defensive project. Like the attack on Lovinac, JF-039 said that the purpose of the attack on Ljubovo was to "cleanse the village and to get the entire population out and to establish a purely Serb territory." As established in rows A17 to A19 of the confidential evidence table, the Ljubovo attack was carried out by men trained at Golubic. And this wasn't some kind of a rogue action on their part. It was a kind of graduation exercise from their Golubic training. In other words, this attack which furthered the common plan was an inherent part of the training at Golubic. The Golubic camp was intended to further the common criminal plan and so was the training conducted there. Your Honours, we've seen that Stanisic and Simatovic had a close relationship and that Stanisic was an astoundingly, to use General Milovanovic's word, well-informed leader. Based on that, Your Honours can be satisfied that Stanisic knew that Simatovic and Martic were in the process of implementing the common criminal plan in the Krajina and that he supported it. Your Honours can also rely on Stanisic's own actions to find that he shared the common criminal plan from the time he made his contributions in the Krajina and the SBWS. A key event in this regard is Stanisic's travel to Dalj in mid-September 1991 to personally intervene in the conduct of the operations to take Vukovar. Your Honours can find further details of this event at rows A20 to A21 of the confidential evidence table. The attack on Dalj, including the expulsion of the Croat population, occurred on 1 August 1991, and had been planned by Hadzic and others for at least several days prior to that. And I refer Your Honours to row A22 of the confidential evidence chart in that regard. This alone proves that the common criminal plan existed prior to September 1991. The intensity of Stanisic's determination in mid-September 1991 that the common goal be achieved as soon as possible supports an inference that he must have shared the goal for some time. So does the fact that he was able to demand on very short notice a meeting with high-level leaders regarding military operations. He certainly wouldn't have been able to do that unless he had been involved in planning for some time. Your Honours can also properly consider evidence of later events to determine what Stanisic's intent was at the time he provided his contributions in the SAO Krajina and SBWS in 1991. P690 records Stanisic talking with Karadzic about exterminating Croats in January 1992. P61 shows that in 1997, Stanisic gave Goran Opacic an award and praised him in front of the rest of the DB special unit. P12 and P990 show that Stanisic celebrated Krajina Security Services Day with Martic, Babic, and Hadzic. And P2667 shows that he congratulated the Krajina security forces on their work going back to 1991. When viewed in light of the extensive evidence of Stanisic's presence in the Krajina, his meetings with Martic, and his assistance in setting up the Krajina security forces, all of this shows that Martic and the other members of the Krajina security services used Stanisic's assistance in precisely the way he intended that it be used. I would now like to deal quickly with the relationship between public security and state security within the Serbian MUP. The Defence make much of this distinction, primarily as an attempt to avoid responsibility for things done by Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza. But the evidence of Stanisic's own witnesses shows that this is nonsense. When asked whether Badza had a productive and co-operative relationship with Stanisic and the Serbian DB, Defence witness Vlado Dragicevic said: "Both sections of the Ministry of the Interior, i.e., the public security and the State Security Services, had a very correct co-operation." And that's at transcript page 14872. Defence witness Nebojsa Bogunovic also gave an example of co-operation between Jovica Stanisic and a public security special unit. That evidence is addressed at rows A23 and A24 of the confidential evidence table. And Your Honours will, of course, recall General Milovanovic's evidence about this relationship. He testified that when he asked Badza who Stanisic was, Badza's answer was "I arrived here with the boss." That's at transcript page 4385. At the very least, the evidence shows that Badza and the accused co-operated, as did public security and state security more generally. And there is nothing surprising about this. There is nothing surprising about two parts of a single ministry co-operating with each other. It is to be expected that they would in the normal course of things. This has arisen as an issue in this case only because the accused seek to distance themselves from their public security colleagues by drawing artificial institutional boundaries that in reality constituted no barrier whatsoever to co-operation. Your Honours, my next point concerns the Defence arguments regarding the tensions among the political leadership of Serbia and the RS set out at pages 300 to 314 of the Stanisic brief. The Defence use this to attempt to defeat liability for the 1995 crimes. In essence, the Defence have provided Your Honours with evidence of tension in the relationship among just three men: Milosevic, Karadzic, and Krajisnik. They then ask Your Honours to conclude based on this evidence that there must have also been a rift in the relationship between the accused and the entirety of the Bosnian Serb leadership as well. This piggybacking argument is an obvious non sequitur, and it is also contrary to the Defence's own evidence. Sir Ivor Roberts, the primary witness that the Defence depend upon to make this argument, made it clear that the tension was among the political leaders and did not include state security. He said: "That was the impression one had for the reasons I was saying earlier, that while the political leaderships were very much out of sympathy with each other, at other levels conversations and understandings continued between state security people and the armies." That's at transcript page 18579. In light of Roberts' testimony, the most that the Defence's evidence might show is that Milosevic, Karadzic, and Krajisnik were no longer effectively co-operating. It tells Your Honours nothing about the accused. In fact, however, the Defence's evidence does not even support a conclusion that Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Milosevic no longer shared a common criminal goal. A closer look at the dispute among these men shows that their disagreement was only about the degree to which the common criminal plan could be achieved and not about the common criminal plan itself. The Defence say that when Milosevic went to Pale to support the Vance-Owen Plan and was subsequently humiliated when it was rejected by the Bosnian Serb parliament, these events led to "a distinct cooling between the governments." But Exhibit P2532 shows that in December 1993, six months after this supposed cooling, Milosevic, Karadzic, and Krajisnik were still able to sit down together to discuss progress towards the achievement of the common criminal plan and to plan military operations. It bears mentioning, of course, that this meeting was hosted by Jovica Stanisic at the DB headquarters. This meeting makes it crystal clear that the disagreement over the peace plan did not represent a rejection of the common criminal plan by any of the members of the JCE. Milosevic's own comments at Pale show the same thing. In his remarks there, he emphasised that the goal was to consolidate what had already been achieved. He praised the Vance-Owen Plan in explicitly nationalistic terms. He encouraged support for it because it offered the Serbs 50 per cent more territory than the Muslims even though their population was 50 per cent less. I refer Your Honours to P3116 at pages 2 and 3. Exhibit P3047 and page 36 of Exhibit P2358 also show that Milosevic's support for the Contact Group Plan and the Dayton plan later was also based on nationalistic considerations. In fact, he sometimes phrased his support for the peace plans in terms of the six strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs. The basic questions Your Honours have to assess in determining liability for the 1995 crimes is whether the common criminal plan still existed. The Defence urge you to conclude that the project of ethnic cleansing had finished by 1993 and that the common criminal plan had therefore ceased. But the events at Srebrenica and Zepa in July 1995 are tragic and incontestable proof that ethnic cleansing had not ended in Bosnia and Herzegovina by the middle of 1993. The murders in Trnovo were an inherent part of that ethnic cleansing. I refer Your Honours to row A25 of the confidential evidence table in connection with Srebrenica and Zepa. Similarly, the charged crimes in Sanski Most show that the process of forcibly and permanently removing non-Serbs, sometimes by killing them, continued there as well. In short, the common criminal plan continued until the last days of the war. The accused's role in the 1995 crimes, which will be discussed by my colleagues, demonstrates beyond reasonable doubt that the accused continued to share this plan. With the Chamber's leave, Mr. Weber will now continue the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As Mr. Groome indicated, I will provide an overview of the special units of the Serbian DB and address the Chamber on matters related to the activities of one of these units, the Red Berets. As part of this discussion, I will address the existence and continuity of the unit between 1991 and 1996 in addition to particular activities of the unit in the Krajina, Bosanski Samac, and Doboj. The special units of the Serbian DB were paramilitary formations deployed by the accused throughout Croatia and Bosnia. Whether it was the Red Berets applying the Doboj experience, the Tigers enforcing Arkan's policy of taking no prisoners in Dalj, or the members of the Skorpions executing six Muslim men and boys at Trnovo, the use of these units furthered a common purpose and resulted in mass devastation to the non-Serb population of the former Yugoslavia. These units acted with impunity, with the blessing and support of the State Security Service of Serbia. The evidence in this case has shown that the Red Berets, Tigers, and Skorpions shared many things in common. The special units shared a common symbol of an upward pointed sword. Their actions were directed by the accused and their subordinates. They operated from nearby bases in Croatia along the border with Serbia in Ilok, Erdut, and Djeletovci, and they participated together in joint operations in both Croatia and Bosnia. Despite their efforts to act in secrecy, despite the attempts of the accused to recycle these efforts to conceal their liability, the evidence consistently demonstrates that Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic contributed these special units in furtherance of the JCE's common criminal purpose. The special units of the Serbian DB often operated in co-ordination with other Serb forces, including the armies, police, and local Territorial Defence units of Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. During these operations, the Serbian DB units were included in joint formations, often referred to as tactical or operational groups. These groups were formed for specific purpose in a limited period of time. The important thing to remember about this is that any resubordinations were temporary and for a particular purpose. This didn't change the fundamental character of the units as DB units loyal to the accused. The fact that the accused willingly and repeatedly gave their men to other JCE members just shows that they were co-operating with those other JCE members and contributing to the overall JCE. Examples of this include the participation of the Red Berets in TG-17 during the take-over of Bosanski Samac, and their participation in TG-Ozren during the take-over of Doboj. Another example is the participation of the Red Berets, Tigers, and Skorpions in Tactical Groups 2 and 3 during Operation Pauk or Spider. In their final trial briefs, the accused seek to mitigate their responsibility for contributing DB special units to joint operations with other Serb forces. An example, the Defence submissions on the participation of Vaso Mijovic and the Red Berets during the 1993 Drina valley operations. As seen on the slide before the Chamber, the Simatovic Defence asserts that Mijovic was within the composition of the VRS. The Stanisic Defence acknowledges Mijovic had some association with Simatovic and claims he had allegiances to many entities. These submissions attempt to obfuscate the fact that the Red Berets trained locals from Bratunac and then participated in combat formations with VRS units at the time. The Prosecution would refer the Chamber to paragraphs 263 through 269 of its brief concerning the involvement of the Red Berets in Bratunac. As the evidence has shown, these co-ordinated joint operations with other military or MUP structures are important because they reflect the accused's intended participation in contribution of special units to other JCE members. It does not make the special units of the Serbian DB formally part of these other structures or diminish their allegiance to the DB as argued by the Defence. Regardless of the level of temporary resubordination with other Serb forces, the accused are responsible for the crimes of their units and those of the other Serb forces because of their contributions to the JCE. Turning to the Red Berets. The accused contributed to the JCE's common purpose by establishing and directing a special DB unit initially referred to by others as Frenki's men and the Knindzas, then often referred to as the Red Berets. The "unit," as it was affectionately called by its members, existed in one form or another from its formation in May 1991 when it was known as a Special Purpose Unit or JPN through its formalisation as the JATD in August 1993, and on to its reincarnation as the JSO in 1996. As Captain Dragan stated twice in Exhibit P2976, the unit existed at all times. Through the testimony of multiple members of the special units of the DB, through DB payment records and personnel files, and through many other witnesses and documentary materials, the Prosecution proved the unit existed at all times and grew over time. In paragraphs 196 to 296 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution discusses the activities of the unit from its inception in 1991 through the Kula award ceremony in 1997, which in the words of Franko Simatovic recorded on video in Exhibit P61 was a "ceremony marking the anniversary of the formation of the Special Operations Unit of the State Security Service." The next words out of the accused's mouth were, "It was constituted on 4 May 1991." The training camps and operations discussed in our brief show a repeated pattern of the accused setting up camps to train unit members and other Serb forces before they were deployed on joint operations where they committed the crimes charged in the indictment. At this stage of the proceedings, it is useful to look at what remains contested and some of the concessions made by the accused in their final trial briefs concerning the Red Berets. Both accused acknowledge in their briefs that the JATD existed after August of 1993. Although they still contest their respective roles in some of the JATD's activities, these challenges are not credible in light of the evidence presented at trial. The Prosecution will not spend much time at this point discussing the unit's activities between 1993 and 1996, but would note a few specific points. In section II of Stanisic's brief entitled "Debunking the mythology that the DB was a war machine," Stanisic portrays himself as a simple civil servant who possessed limited operative resources. These submission ignore the fact that the Serbian DB was devoting funds and resources to their special units through various forms of payment. As examples of cash expenditures on the JATD, the Prosecution would refer the Trial Chamber to row B1 of the confidential evidence chart. The JATD also had priority in terms of staffing. As an example of the preferential treatment in the staffing of the JATD by the accused Stanisic, the Prosecution would refer the Chamber to row B2 of the confidential evidence chart. And also at this time for Your Honours, the Prosecution would additionally refer the Chamber to page 2 of Slobodan Milosevic's 2001 appeal concerning the Serbian government's expenditures on weapons, ammunition, and equipment for the VRS, RSK, and special anti-terrorist forces. The appeal is Exhibit P3023. The Prosecution requests that the next slide not be broadcast to the public. The personnel files of unit members further illustrate that the Red Berets were built and used for combat. All parties in this case tendered personnel files. Here, on slide 40 are some references from the personnel files tendered by the Defence. Even these files show the commander of the unit was Franko Simatovic, and the functions of unit members described repeatedly as soldiers including commanding platoons and combat groups. The files tendered by the Defence also demonstrate that the unit provided combat training, engaged in combat operations, and sent unit members to the front line. DB payment records, personnel files of unit members, and even the DB's own reports all show the priority of Stanisic was to support a combat unit commanded by Simatovic. Your Honours, I don't know if you're anticipating taking a break at this time or if you'd like me to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As the commander of the unit, Simatovic was a powerful and well-connected man. If Simatovic was some low functionary as he claims throughout his brief, unit members like Dejan Sliskovic would not have considered him their commander. We would also not see him sharing a couch with Martic, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Zupljanin, and Stanisic as we see in Exhibit P391. Nor would he have attended planning meetings for military operations like the February 1993 meeting with senior leadership of the VRS and VJ regarding Operation Udar as P392 shows he did. The Prosecution would additionally refer the Chamber to rows B3 to B7 of the confidential evidence chart. Thought the Defence cases and their final trial briefs, both accused challenged the continuity of the unit between 1991 up until its formalisation as the JATD in 1993. Before discussing evidence related to the unit's early existence, the Prosecution would like to note some additional statements by the accused Stanisic in his find brief. In paragraphs 497 and 514, Stanisic makes a number of concessions with respect to the unit's existence prior to 1993. Some of these statements are now on the slide before the Chamber. In paragraph 497, Stanisic acknowledges that he had control over a unit known as the Red Berets between August-September 1991 until the end of February 1992 as "part of his aim to create an anti-terrorist unit, ATU." And "Stanisic intended to use the 28 selected to create an ATU." By making these concessions, Stanisic is not challenging the Prosecution's case that he had the authority to create and control the DB special unit known as the Red Berets at some point prior to his official appointment as chief of the service in 1992. He is also not challenging the Prosecution's case that a DB unit known as the Red Berets existed prior to its reformation as the JATD, albeit in a limited form for a six- to seven -month period. The evidence in this case does not support these limited conclusions, and it shows the unit existed at all times from May 1991 onwards. As a general observation, Stanisic tries to redesignate his Red Berets between 1991 and 1992 as the ATU throughout his brief. However, this is not what the unit was commonly referred to in documents prior to 1993. As seen in a significant quantity of materials admitted in this case, it was often referred to as the Special Purpose Unit of the MUP Serbia, a unit, the evidence shows, existed between 1991 and 1993 until being renamed the JATD. The Prosecution provides references to examples of these documents in row B8 of the confidential evidence chart. In paragraphs 37 to 63 of his brief, Stanisic acknowledges some of the individuals who were present in Fruska Gora for portions of either 1991 or 1992, including unit members Laka, Pilipovic, Borjan Vuckovic, and the Bozic brothers. These were all individuals who joined the unit in Golubic prior to August 1991. The Prosecution would refer the Chamber to Annex A of its brief for further description of evidence related to these unit members. With Your Honours' leave, the Prosecution requests to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The evidence in this case also shows that not all members of the unit were in Fruska Gora and Pajzos after July 1991. Milan Babic, JF-031 and JF-039 all provided evidence that unit members continued their operations in the Krajina after Golubic. Milan Babic testified that Frenki's base, a base of the Serbian DB, was in Korenica after August 1991. This can be found on page 335 of P1878. The Prosecution would additionally refer the Chamber to rows B19 to B24 of the confidential evidence chart. Simatovic himself admits to the continuing involvement of the DB in the Krajina during the Kula awards ceremony when he stated that: "The unit provided important support in the liberation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." He then stated: "Around 5.000 soldiers were engaged in these battles, and their actions were co-ordinated by the unit command and intelligence team from the 2nd Administration." In other words, the accused used people from the 2nd Administration along with unit members to co-ordinate the actions of other Serb forces who were controlled by Milan Martic. Before continuing with further submissions on the continuity of the unit, the Prosecution would briefly make a few points about two witnesses relied upon in the Defence briefs and related to the events in the Krajina. The first, Aco Draca. He greatly minimised evidence related to the conduct of the accused and Milan Martic. During cross-examination, the witness displayed his bias, and the Chamber had to caution the witness on repeated occasions to provide complete answers and tell the whole truth about interactions between the Krajina and Serbian DBs. For example, he testified that there were rumours of Rade Kostic working for the Serbian DB, but he couldn't remember who said that to him. He later acknowledged that he knew that Milan Martic himself had claimed that. On this occasion, he was cautioned by the Chamber to tell the whole truth. On another occasion, he absolutely asserted that there was never a plan or proposal to join the RSK DB to the Serbian DB. He later acknowledged that Milan Martic frequently proposed the very same idea to him. Specific examples of his unreliable testimony can also be found in his evidence related to the charged crimes in the indictment. Draca portrayed the crimes committed in Bruska as a private feud between a few citizens on direct examination. He stated at page 16765 that the villagers from Bruska were interviewed by the Krajina police and "no statements were taken from them." Admitted in evidence as P43 is an official record of an interview completed by the Benkovac SJB, the very station that Draca worked for. This record includes the account of Jasna Denona just four days after the murders charged in the indictment and shows that the Benkovac SJB possessed information that the Krajina police were the perpetrators of the murders in Bruska. This witness's evidence related to the perpetrators of the Skabrnja massacre is also inaccurate when compared to other exhibits, such as D675, which does not reference the 63rd Parachute Brigade as being one of the JNA units engaged in these operations. Draca's evidence regarding Skabrnja is also contradicted by Prosecution Exhibits 2802, 1212, and 1209. The second witness, Goran Opacic, was convicted for the crimes committed in Skabrnja according to Exhibit P3106 and P3107. In his brief, Simatovic does not rely upon Opacic's evidence related to the massacre in Skabrnja but instead relies upon his denials that the accused were involved with the training and activities of Serb forces in the Krajina. This witness is wholly uncredible. For example, he claimed to never have any interactions with Stanisic before the Kula award ceremony in 1997. However, as you can see on slide number 47 before you, Stanisic greeted Opacic unlike many of the other members of the unit at Kula with a kiss, and then during his unscripted remarks at the ceremony Opacic was the first person mentioned by Stanisic out of all the members of the unit present that day. When confronted with his prominent role during the presentation of awards at page 18313, the witness provided an unconvincing answer about his exchange with Stanisic. His answer is provided on slide number 48. Even this witness's own brother and fellow unit member admitted in Exhibit P2984 that he was "co-operating with the RDB from the very beginning via the Golubic camp." Returning to the continuity of the unit between 1991 and 1993, as already seen, Stanisic acknowledges that the Red Berets existed during the fall of 1991 and spring of 1992. There were individuals who joined the unit during this time that are centrally relevant to this case. Two of these individuals, both relevant to the crimes committed in Bosanski Samac where Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, and Aleksandar Vukovic. Crni joined the unit in October 1991 as part of the unit's active service. His personnel file shows that by February 1992, Crni was based in Lezimir as the commander of the 1st Rifle Squad. In P2984, another report by Zivojin Ivanovic from December 1991 indicates that Crni had been stationed in Ilok. According to Stevan Todorovic in P1576, Aleksandar Vukovic was one of the instructors with the DB special unit in Ilok before being deployed to Bosanski Samac. A document from Vukovic's personnel records admitted as P3154 further confirms he was a member of the unit in February 1992 and joined an assistant machine-gunner. Both Crni and Vukovic are mentioned in a December 1992 entry from the Mladic notebooks. This entry reflects a meeting between Mladic and members of the Samac municipality, including Stevan Todorovic. On slide 50, are Mladic's notes of what Todorovic said at the meeting. Todorovic stated that there were men sent to Ilok for training and on 18 April 1992, they were transferred together on helicopters with 30 volunteers from Kragujevac and among them were two members of the Serbian MUP, Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, and Aleksandar Vukovic. This exhibit represents significant corroboration of the 92 quater testimony of Todorovic and shows that locals from Samac were sent to Ilok for training by the Serbian MUP and then returned to Bosnia with former SRS volunteers and members of the Serbian MUP. In conjunction with other evidence related to Crni, Vukovic, and Ilok, it is clear that the DB were the ones who provided this training and oversaw the perpetrators of crimes upon their deployment to Bosanski Samac in April 1992. During their deployment to Bosanski Samac, the individuals who were trained in Ilok considered themselves to be part of a unit called the Grey Wolves and Red Berets. Stanisic attacks the credibility of JF-047 and attempts to distinguish the Grey Wolves from the Red Berets as being associated to two different units in paragraphs 588 to 592 of his brief. They were not two different units. As seen on the slide before the Chamber, the Grey Wolf patch worn by the unit is admitted as P141. The same emblem was also placed on the unit's own forms as seen in Exhibit P2786. Also depicted on the slide the Wolf insignia was used by the Red Berets on the wall of the Kula centre to show the location of -- locations of their operations. In P2976, the same Wolf symbol was worn by Simatovic on his own red beret. The Prosecution would additionally refer the Chamber to row B25 of the confidential evidence chart. In paragraph 278 of its brief, the Prosecution discusses the unit members who were killed during operations prior to 1993. Serbian DB extended posthumous awards or payments to many of these individuals. These recognitions further illustrate that the unit continually existed between 1991 and 1993. The Prosecution requests that the next slide not be broadcast to the public. One of these individuals was Milan Dimic, a unit member who was killed in Doboj on 13 July 1992, one day after approximately 27 non-Serb civilians were removed from Percin's Disco and killed while forming part of a human shield for the Red Berets and other Serb forces. For his efforts, the Serbian DB extended 62 payments to Dimic's relatives between 1993 and 1995 and recognised him with an award in 1996, which is noted on the slide before the Chamber. Between April and July 1992, other members of the unit were also involved in the training in Ozren and operations in Doboj. Three witnesses in this case all name Raja Bozovic and Davor Subotic, aka Riki, as possessing a commanding role in these operations. The Prosecution would refer the Chamber to rows B26 to B29 of the confidential evidence chart. And, Your Honours, again with your leave if we could please turn to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Both accused argue that they only did things that they were permitted or required to do by the Serbian law and certain regulations. For example, at paragraph 100 of his brief, Stanisic claims that he was a "stickler for rules." The next 25 pages of his brief analyses those rules and requests an inference that Stanisic did only the things permitted by the regulations. This argument is contradicted by the accused's own concession that an anti-terrorist unit was formed between 1991 and 1992 and did exist after the fall of 1993. There is no provision in any of the relevant laws or regulations permitting the DB to form an armed unit. Nevertheless, the evidence has shown that they did. Lastly. Stanisic Defence weaves arguments about notice throughout its final trial brief. With respect to the Stanisic Defence claim that the only unit sufficiently pled is the "28 elite trainers," the Prosecution asserts that the special units of the Serbian DB which were the focus of this case were clearly set out in the indictment, particularly paragraphs 4 and 6, and that is consistent with the evidence presented by the Prosecution. With respect to the Defence contention that the names of certain individuals contained in the evidence tendered by the Prosecution are material fact which should have been pled in the indictment, the Defence confuses evidence with material facts. The third amended indictment pled the material facts which underpin the charges in a manner sufficient to inform the accused of the charges and allow him to prepare his defence. The names individuals, whether physical perpetrators or tools or simply otherwise relevant individuals are a matter of evidence. At this time, Ms. Friedman will continue the Prosecution's submissions with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused are liable for the deployment and operations of Arkan's SDG in numerous locations, including in SBWS, Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Sanski Most, where they committed the charged crimes which were the object of the JCE. I will begin by speaking about the credibility of Prosecution Witness JF-057 and Defence Witnesses Dmitrovic and Pelevic in relation to Arkan's connection to and reliance on the Serbian DB. Those are the first two items listed on slide 56 before you. I will next discuss issues related to SBWS. First, Simatovic's liability for crimes, item 3, and then three points in relation to Stanisic's liability, items 4 through 6. My final three points relate to the Bijeljina and Zvornik crime bases. I will now move into private session for approximately five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could you please adjust your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Dimitrijevic testified that Srdjan Golubic, the SDG member depicted in P605 kicking civilians lying on the street in Bijeljina, was punished for his conduct by removal from the SDG. He emphasised that this kind of conduct was unacceptable in the SDG. Only when confronted on cross-examination by the fact that Golubic appeared on a DB payment list from 1995, did Dimitrijevic acknowledge that it was practice that people were forgiven some time. Witness Pelevic cannot be considered a witness of truth in light of his more than evident admiration towards Arkan whom he still considers to be a hero of the Serbian people. This admiration led to biased and dishonest evidence as demonstrated by his statement that he never heard of crimes being committed by Arkan or members of the SDG and SBWS and affirmed that he had still not heard of such things even at the time that he testified. Pelevic offered evidence that was demonstrably false. When asked whether the SDG ever participated in combat with the Skorpions, Pelevic answered "no, never." The Prosecution has tendered video footage of joint operations seen on P483 as well as additional documentary and witness evidence. It is highly unlikely that Pelevic did not know about joint operations between these units. And even if it were the case that he did not have actual knowledge and chose to remain wilfully blind as he claims to have done in respect of Arkan's criminal record, that, too, should preclude any reliance being placed on testimony he offered. In another instance, Pelevic asserted that he was sure that nobody from the Serbian MUP or DB came to the Erdut training centre while also stating that Badza often came to the Erdut training centre. Your Honours will find this at T-16337 to 16338. Giving Pelevic the benefit of the doubt of what he knew at the time of the events, he must have later learned that even when Badza first arrived to the region and commanded the TO, he was also a high profile employee of the Serbian MUP, yet he unabashedly provided evidence that no one from the Serbian MUP came to the Erdut training centre because he was determined to provide evidence which distanced the SDG from the Serbian DB. Simatovic argues that there is no evidence linking him to Arkan and cites Gagic's evidence that he never saw him in Slavonia. There is certainly -- there is certainly more evidence of Simatovic's personal presence in Krajina than of his presence in SBWS. It is important to bear in mind that the charged crimes in these two regions were occurring simultaneously. Simatovic is responsible for the crimes in SBWS because they were part of the common criminal plan and he was a member of the JCE. His main contribution at that point in time was in the Krajina, and that was a significant contribution to the JCE. Simatovic made contributions in the SBWS as well by setting up bases there and participating in the attack on Vukovar; yet, even if he had not made a significant contribution in SBWS, his liability for the crimes rests firmly on his participation in the JCE. Both Defence teams have accepted the evidence that Badza and Arkan co-operated closely in the SBWS. The Defence attempt to dispute the link between Arkan and the DB in two ways. First, by breaking the link between the public security and state security, or Stanisic and Badza, and secondly, by discounting the evidence that DB operatives were acting on Stanisic's behalf. Stanisic emphasises Badza's presence and claims that his own absence is significant. However, the fact that Badza was actually deployed to SBWS in the fall of 1991 does not diminish Stanisic's responsibility. First, Stanisic was present in the region at key moments and was very well informed about what was occurring there. Second, Stanisic co-operated closely with Badza and the other JCE members, including Hadzic, Milosevic, Bogdanovic, and Arkan. Third, Stanisic ensured that the men he was in charge of, including Kostic and Kojic, provided vital assistance to JCE members Hadzic, Badza, and Arkan who were on the ground in SBWS. The Stanisic brief at page -- paragraph 417 claims that there is "not a single piece of reliable evidence to support the assertion that Badza took orders or even advice from Stanisic." Stanisic would apparently dismiss the evidence of General Milovanovic referred to earlier by Mr. Farr and which appears now on slide 65. The only reasonable inference based on General Milovanovic's evidence is that when Badza said, "I arrived here with the boss," he was referring to Stanisic. In cross-examination, the Defence challenge this evidence on the basis that according to their de jure positions, Stanisic should not have been Badza's boss. This is an example of where the evidence of what actually transpired portrays a situation that is different than what the laws dictated. Milovanovic's evidence about this meeting in which he found Stanisic's knowledge to be astounding attests to Stanisic's role in planning and co-ordinating actions in furtherance of the JCE on behalf of the Serbian government and explains why he may have functioned as Badza's boss even though, legally speaking, Badza was not subordinated to him. The Prosecution requests that the next slide not be broadcast. Even putting aside the evidence that Stanisic had de facto authority over Badza, this is but one instance where Stanisic attempts to elevate the Prosecution's evidentiary burden by suggesting that the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt certain facts which are not necessary in order to prove the accused's responsibility. The fact is that Stanisic and Badza as heads of state security and public security of the Serbian MUP worked closely with Milosevic and co-operated with each other during the indictment period providing significant Serbian MUP resources to the other JCE members. Slides 66 and 67 contain examples of the evidence Your Honours have heard about the co-operation between the state security and public security, both between the heads of the services and members operating in the field. Sliskovic provides evidence about co-operation between members of the SAJ unit under Badza and the JATD under Stanisic and Simatovic, which is corroborated further by the interview with Obrad Stevanovic, contained in P973, and other operations -- and other evidence of joint operations that Ms. Harbour will discuss. It is also important to bear in mind that references to the Serbian MUP do not refer only to public security. The Serbian MUP contains two divisions, the public security and state security, and a reference to the Serbian MUP can refer to either of them. The Prosecution requests that the next slide not be broadcast. Slide number 68 contains two documents which refer to DB members as employees of the Serbian MUP without further specification. Furthermore, it is apparent in the evidence that individuals who were not closely affiliated with the DB may not have known whether a particular person worked for public security or state security due to their intertwined activities. I refer the Chamber, for example, to the evidence of Borivoje Savic at T-1876. Perhaps the best example of the intertwined nature of the services is Kojic's statement, P1698, seen on slide 69, wherein he asserts that even while he was officially employed by the Serbian MUP public security, he was actually answering to Stanisic. I will now move to a discussion of Stanisic's responsibility for the acts of his subordinates as they relate to his liability for crimes in SBWS and in Bijeljina and Zvornik. Stanisic argues at paragraph 734 that the Prosecution has not shown evidence that Stanisic provided instructions or orders to Kostic or that Kostic's actions were in furtherance of a DB policy and suggests that the Prosecution is inappropriately resting liability on an employment relationship. The Prosecution has demonstrated that Kostic actions were carried out in accordance with how Stanisic intended to use the Serbian DB to further the JCE. The Prosecution does not need to produce evidence of an order directly from Stanisic to Kostic in order to meet its burden of proof. Stanisic was the man in charge, and as such he could be expected to be well informed. But he was even better informed than expected. Mr. Farr has discussed this issue recounting evidence from Witnesses Milovanovic and Corbic. I will provide you with two more examples of this evidence. In January 1992, Stanisic affirmed to Karadzic that he had the ability to appoint people in SBWS. Excerpts from this conversation appear on slide 71. Stanisic discussed having been present in the field in order to talk to commanders and states that he would be responsible for creating "some kind of concept." Defence Witness Knezevic testified at T-13542 that Stanisic had a conversation with him about the situation in SBWS when Stanisic was passing through the area. He asked Knezevic to confirm certain information that he had received from DB operative Lazar Sarac. This shows that Stanisic had personal knowledge of information reported by DB operatives who were several levels beneath him in the DB hierarchy and that he actively sought additional information. The only reasonable inference based on Stanisic's level of knowledge and personal involvement is that the actions of his employees were pursuant to the direction in which he led the Serbian DB. It is clear that he established a policy of helping the Serb forces perpetrate JCE crimes. I would like to move into private session for approximately eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The words and actions of Milan Martic offer further evidence of Kostic's association with Stanisic. I refer Your Honours to the intercepted conversation P1605 on slide 73. In this call, Martic irately implores Milosevic to have Stanisic removed Kostic and the rest of what he refers to as Stanisic's gang from Erdut and Pajzos. Milosevic denies that these men are Stanisic's men, but in fact Kostic's personnel file leaves no doubt that he was working for Stanisic at that time. Simatovic referred to Kostic at the Kula camp celebration as a "distinguished member of this unit." I will now discuss several issues in relation to the accused's liability for the Zvornik crime base. The Defence again argued that the crimes were planned and carried out by other JCE members without their involvement. The Prosecution requests that the next slide not be broadcast. In trying to dismiss the evidence that Marko Pavlovic, commander of the Zvornik TO, was a member of the Serbian DB, Stanisic attempts to challenge the evidence of three witnesses at paragraph 739 of his brief, claiming that the evidence of each is uncorroborated when in fact they are three independent sources of evidence that corroborate each other as summarised in slide number 75. First, the Stanisic's brief misstates JF-061's evidence. Stanisic states that according to JF-061, Pavlovic claimed to have a DB ID, which is a clear indication of the falsity of his claims. Your Honours can see what JF-061 actually said in the confidential evidence table at row C1; thus the evidence is not that Pavlovic claimed to have a card issued by the DB. B-161 provides evidence of Pavlovic's close relationship with Tepavcevic which Your Honours will find at rows C2 and C3 of the confidential evidence table. Stanisic urges the Chamber to dismiss this evidence which he claims is uncorroborated. This applies an overly stringent approach. It is not necessary for another witness to offer the exact same facts. Evidence of a connection with Tepavcevic is evidence of a connection with the DB. Stanisic then asks the Chamber to disregard JF-026's evidence by asserting that JF-026 retracted his evidence that Tepavcevic was Pavlovic's boss. First this assertion is erroneous since JF-026's evidence was about Kostic, not Pavlovic. Further, JF-026 did not retract this evidence altogether. JF-026's testimony was that Kostic worked for the Serbian MUP but he could no longer remember the name of his superior at the time. JF-026 also testified that Pavlovic referred to Kostic as his boss, which is another point of corroboration and his connection to the DB. JF-026 also offered evidence which indirectly bolsters B-161's credibility and attests to the independence of these two witnesses. Your Honours will find that evidence and brief confidential arguments at rows C4 to C6 of the confidential evidence table. As he did with Kostic, Stanisic argues that actions committed by Tepavcevic cannot be impugned to Stanisic. The Prosecution submits that the fact that Tepavcevic was Stanisic's deputy leads to a strong inference that he was acting pursuant to Stanisic's directions. I will discuss just one piece of evidence that makes this the only reasonable inference. In December 1993, a meeting that was attended by the key leaders from Serbia and Republika Srpska was hosted at the DB headquarters in Belgrade. This meeting was discussed in detail during the Prosecution's 98 bis submissions and earlier by Mr. Farr. It is Exhibit P2532 and is on slide 77. At this time, I would simply draw Your Honours' attention to the Serbian MUP attendees of this meeting who were Sokolovic, Stanisic, Badza, and Tepavcevic. Stanisic presided over the meeting, and Sokolovic and Badza both spoke during different points in time; whereas Tepavcevic outranked by all these men did not. The meeting demonstrates Stanisic's intent to use the resources available to him to contribute to the JCE on the territory of the Republika Srpska, as well as the fact that Tepavcevic was well aware of this. With respect to Stanisic's liability for the crimes in Zvornik the Stanisic Defence brief at paragraphs 771 to 772 asks the question: Why would Stanisic be involved in the take-over of Zvornik and arrange supplies for paramilitaries only to later arrest the Vuckovic brothers for crimes. The possible answer to the question, if the evidence that the arrest occurred at Stanisic's behest is believed, is that he felt compelled to do so for political reasons. The arrests occurred more than a year and a half later, at a time when reports about the crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina were being published. The arrest of only two individuals is insignificant in light of the evidence of the DB's involvement in those crimes. The more telling question is why these were the only arrests that were made at that time. Both of the Vuckovic brothers in their statements to the DB provided information about heinous crimes perpetrated by Marko Pejic, one of Arkan's men. I refer Your Honours to an excerpt of Vojin Vuckovic's statement, P2987, which appears at row C7 of the confidential evidence table.
