utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, before the break I referred you to Vojin Vuckovic's statement which implicates Marko Pejic, one of Arkan's SDGs -- SDG members in crimes in Zvornik. Not only did the Serbian DB fail arrest Pejic on the basis of this information, they issued per diem payments to him as a member of the SDG. Pejic's name appears at page 30 of Exhibit P541 and page 8 of P543. These are JATD payment lists for the period leading up to the Sanski Most operations from mid-August to mid-September 1995. Finally, Your Honours, the report compiled by Milorad Davidovic in August 1992 about the situation in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Brcko provides additional evidence of the Serbian DB's involvement in sending men to Eastern Bosnia. Excerpts from this important piece of evidence appear on slide 79. The Davidovic report demonstrates that members of the unit operated alongside member of the SDG in "liberating these areas" and discusses the involvement of the Serbian MUP in sending these and other forces. Another passage at page 10 conveys Ivanovic's statement that his group was sent by Simatovic and Tepavcevic. Your Honours, it is significant that Serbian DB employees and associates who operated under Stanisic's direction appeared wherever Arkan appeared. Whether it be Kostic and Kojic in SBWS, Kostic and Pavlovic in Zvornik, or Dragan Filipovic in Sanski Most as Ms. Harbour will discuss. The Prosecution has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Stanisic and Simatovic used the resources and personnel at their disposal to make a significant contribution to the crimes charged in SBWS, Bijeljina, and Zvornik. Ms. Harbour will now continue the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to introduce the third special unit of the Serbian DB, the Skorpions. I will then discuss the joint operations that the unit, SDG, and Skorpions participated in together from 1994 until the end of the indictment period. The evidence of these operations reveals how Stanisic and Simatovic used these units to further the common purpose. I will conclude with a discussion of Sanski Most, particularly the SDG's operations and crimes there. All of these operations depended upon the co-ordination of different JCE members and the organs they controlled, demonstrating that JCE members continued to pursue the common criminal purpose throughout the indictment period. The evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that are both accused are criminally responsible for the charged crimes in Trnovo and Sanski Most. My first point and an overarching theme of my submissions is that the accused were responsible for the Skorpions. Stanisic and Simatovic controlled the Skorpions during the indictment period, using them for special operations in Croatia and Bosnia. Slobodan Medic, the Skorpion's commander, referred to Stanisic as his boss and took orders from both accused from at least 1994. Slide 82 sets out some of the evidence showing that the Skorpions were a special unit of the Serbian DB and controlled by both accused. This corroborates the evidence of JF-024 and Stoparic which both Defence teams have challenged in their final trial briefs. In addition to, the evidence of the Skorpions' joint operations with the SDG and JATD in 1994 and 1995 unequivocally demonstrates that Stanisic and Simatovic were controlling the Skorpions' movements during this entire period: Before, during, and after the Trnovo murders. The evidence of these operations also reveals how the accused contributed to the JCE through the Skorpions, SDG, and JATD. I will address the three successive operations in turn, beginning with Operation Pauk. As stated in the Prosecution's final trial brief, Operation Pauk was significant for two main reasons. One, it exemplifies the close co-ordination between JCE members pursuing the common purpose during this period; and two, it is the first in a series of actions where the accused deployed members of all three of the DB special units into combat together. The accused do not dispute that Stanisic was involved in meetings with high-level leaders before and during Operation Pauk. The Mladic notebooks reflect several meetings where the attendees discuss Stanisic's contribution of manpower to Pauk as reflected on slide 84. At a meeting on 7 October 1994, Stanisic promised to send Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: On 8 November, both accused attended a meeting where Stanisic said he had "provided forces strong enough to ensure the liberation of Velika Kladusa and Fikret Abdic's return there." Indeed, around this time the Skorpions, SDG, and JATD deployed to Pauk. I refer Your Honours to slide 85. Zoran Rajic escorted the Skorpions across the border from Serbia into Bosnia and oversaw their activities in Pauk. Witnesses Sliskovic and JF-024 discussed this in their evidence. The Stanisic Defence argues that Operation Pauk was a legitimate, lawfully conducted operation. Curiously, they then argue at paragraph 1032 of their brief that Mladic attempted to implicate Stanisic by the notebook entries showing that Stanisic was personally involved in sending Arkan's men and the Skorpions into this operation. The Stanisic Defence fails to explain how implicating Stanisic in what they consider to be an entirely legitimate and lawfully conducted operation would benefit Mladic. The Simatovic Defence does not dispute that Simatovic was present in Petrova Gora during the Pauk operations on multiple occasions, but they argue that Simatovic's role in Pauk was limiting to -- limited to setting up radio surveillance. Similarly, the Stanisic Defence argues that Stanisic's only role in the Pauk command involved "members of the JATD involved in security." Viewed in its totality, the evidence tells a different story. Slide 86 sets out evidence that Stanisic and Simatovic spent a significant amount of time in Petrova Gora, that the Pauk commander Novakovic reported to Stanisic on the operation's progress, and that both accused gave orders to and met with Bozovic and Legija, the commanders of TG-2 and TG-3. Bozovic and Legija in turn commanded the JATD, the SDG, and the Skorpions in combat. The Stanisic Defence agrees that Bozovic was a reserve JATD member during Pauk, while the Simatovic Defence relies on Witness Plahuta's claim that Bozovic never belonged to the JATD. An official JATD note, P3024, describes JATD members' involvement in ambush, sniping, combat training, and identification of "targets for our operations." The document sets out the combat equipment used, the combat equipment issued to both Bozovic and Legija, evidence of these two individuals' relationship to the Serbian DB. Stanisic argues that this was probably the only time the JATD engaged in such activities. In light of the totality of the evidence, this argument does not hold water. The Prosecution requests that the next slide not be broadcast. The Serbian DB's payment lists for the Pauk period reveal the level of their financial investment in the Pauk operation and their logistical involvement in transferring funds that Abdic provided for the units involved. The Simatovic Defence has pointed out that the Serbian DB's payment lists included commanders, pilots, and other members of the Army of the Republic of Serb Krajina who were involved in the operation. In addition, groups of JATD members were paid on the same list as Bozovic, and groups of Tigers were paid on the same list as Legija during this period, as indicated on slide 87. Rajic was also paid during this period that he was overseeing the Skorpions in Pauk. Simatovic personally signed some of these payment lists. The fact that the Skorpions do not appear on any Serbian DB payment lists for this or any other period indicates that they may not have been paid by the DB through this vehicle. Their absence from the payment lists does not negate the incontrovertible evidence of their involvement in the Pauk under Legija's TG-2 and the totality of the evidence that they were there at the behest of the accused. Let us now turn to the Trnovo-Treskavica operation, shortly after Pauk, where JATD member Mijovic commanded the SDG and Skorpions. During this operation, the Skorpions shot six Muslim men and boys in cold blood while one of them videotaped the entire event. Both Defence final trial briefs discuss a meeting that took place before the operation at Badza's office at the Serbian MUP attended by Kojic, Badza, Medic, Arkan, Mrgud, and Ljubo Milojavic, the Plavi Brigade commander. At this meeting, Badza said the Skorpions, SDG, and Plavi Brigade should be sent to Trnovo to assist the VRS in combat. Simatovic then contacted Arkan in Erdut and arranged for the SDG's participation. I refer Your Honours to P1666 and the confidential evidence table, items D9 to D11. Kojic ultimately led these three units into Trnovo as indicated in items D12 and D13 on the confidential evidence table. As shown on slide 89 and discussed by Ms. Friedman, Kojic was an official DB employee who by his own account was reporting directly to Stanisic. Through his involvement at the pre-deployment meeting and in leading these units, Kojic was responsible to the accused. During the operations, prominent JATD member Mijovic commanded the three units. Mijovic was a long-time member of the unit and directly subordinate to the accused as indicated by the evidence on slide 90. His leadership role in the Trnovo-Treskavica operation is evidence that Stanisic and Simatovic were behind this operation. Throughout their involvement in the Trnovo-Treskavica operations, Skorpions, Plavi, and SDG were consistently referred to as Serbian MUP units in official military and police reports as indicated on slides 91 and 92. The Defence offers several arguments to distance the Serbian DB from these units. The Simatovic Defence argues that the documents referring to Serbian MUP units are mistaken and that Karadzic had requested the assistance. The Stanisic Defence argues that these were called Serbian MUP units because they were subject to Badza and the public security and had nothing to do with the accused and the DB. Stanisic's final trial brief is very misleading, asserting that both JF-029 and JF-024 testified that the Skorpions were reserve forces of the SAJ of public security. Both witnesses were testifying about the 1998 to 1999 period. Aside from this misleading assertion, the Defence's characterisation of Karadzic and Badza's involvement arises from the evidence and is a crucial part of the Prosecution's case, demonstrating the JCE members' deep involvement in furthering the common purpose through the Skorpions' crimes in Trnovo. Nevertheless, the totality of the evidence and the prominent role the accused's subordinates Kojic and Mijovic played in the Trnovo operations precludes any interpretation that would exclude the Serbian DB's authority over the Skorpions. Both accused challenge the evidence that Mijovic commanded these units in the Trnovo-Treskavica operations. In light of all the evidence, the Defence challenges should be dismissed. And I would like to ask if we can go into private session for approximately two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The next two pieces of evidence are on slide 94 and must be considered together. P1454 is an order from Mladic on 1 July 1995 in response to a 30 June dispatch from the "MUP of Serbia's ATD unit." Mladic orders "inform us through proper channels if anyone is seriously wounded in the Trnovo sector." This order was sent to the organs whose subsequent reports refer to the Skorpions, SDG, and Plavi in the Trnovo operations as Serbian MUP units as I previously discussed. The next document, P1084, is a document on Serbian MUP ATD unit letterhead signed by Mijovic as commander and delivered to the RS MUP in Pale on 19 July 1995. It states that "the ATD unit of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia was ordered to pull back from the zone of combat operations in the Trnova sector by 1200 hours on 20 July 1995." Together, it is clear from these two documents that (a) the Serbian MUP ATD unit was active in Trnovo; and (b), Mijovic was its commander. The evidence reveals that the Skorpions pulled out of Trnovo five days after Mijovic's dispatch. These documents independently corroborate the two witnesses I've discussed regarding Mijovic's role in Trnovo, commanding Serbian MUP units in July 1995. Another corroborating piece of evidence is P2966, page 7, the testimony of Tomislav Kovac in the Skorpions trial in Belgrade. He testified that Vaso Mijovic was the Skorpions' commander in Trnovo. The Prosecution relies on this evidence only to the extent that it corroborates the other evidence I have just discussed, taking the Defence point that Kovac was not cross-examined before this Chamber. I will now discuss the SBWS operations after Operation Storm when the accused pulled the Skorpions, SDG, and JATD together once again. In September 1995 and thereafter, the accused held meetings in the SBWS with high-level military officials. I refer Your Honours to slide 96. By early September, following an approach similar to that taken in Pauk, three operational groups were formed of the DB special units and SVK units. Mijovic co-operated with the OG-1 Baranja command and provided soldiers trained by the JATD. Legija led OG-2, leading around 250 SDG in Eastern Slavonia, and Zvezdan Jovanovic was deputy commander of OG-3 which included the Skorpions and covered Western Srem. I refer Your Honours to P1080. The pattern of the Skorpions deployments in 1994 and 1995 demonstrates that they were a unit under the accused's control. For a year they were deployed into consecutive operations with the SDG and JATD. For each operation, the Skorpions were subordinated to a member of a DB special unit, first Legija in Pauk, then Mijovic in Trnovo, and finally Jovanovic in the SBWS. For Pauk and Trnovo, DB members Rajic and Kojic escorted them across borders into the combat zone. Both Defence teams cling heavily onto evidence that the Skorpions were a unit of the SVK under General Loncar. As shown and slide 97, P3096 shows that whatever their relationship with the SVK, the accused ultimately controlled the Skorpions' assignments. On 28 August 1995, Bozovic and other members of the unit took over command of the SVK security organs and provided the Skorpions, called the Boco Squad, to escort the SVK officials out of town. On 30 October 1995, the SVK reported "The Serbia State Security is in charge now, 'Frenki,' Jovica. Loncar is nothing but a pawn now." In light of the totality of the evidence, there can be no reasonable doubt that the Skorpions were acting as tools of the accused when they persecuted and then murdered six Bosniaks near Trnovo. As the Skorpions, SDG, and JATD units were forming operational groups to prepare for combat in SBWS, Arkan led a SDG unit into operations around Sanski Most and Banja Luka. Arkan and the SDG rounded up non-Serb civilians at the Sanus Hotel and then murdered them in groups in the areas of Sasina and Trnova on 20 and 21 September 1995. I will now discuss the accused's liability for these murders, first through the lens of the Mladic notebooks and then through the lens of the DB payment lists. Both Defence teams seek to distance the accused from Arkan and the SDG's activities in Sanski Most. They argue that Arkan was in Sanski Most at the behest of Karadzic and the SDS leadership and working with the RS MUP. Stanisic also points out that the RS government requested Badza to supply men for the operations, resulting in some 400 PJPs being sent from Serbia where they were also resubordinated to the RS MUP. The evidence on which the Defence relies is important and relevant to reveal the deep involvement that JCE members Karadzic, Mico Stanisic, Badza, Mladic, and others had in perpetuating the common criminal purpose along with Arkan in these operations. The evidence is clear that Stanisic and Simatovic were also intimately involved in these operations, and I particularly draw the Chamber's attention to a series of Mladic notebook entries in September and October 1995. On slide 100, P2543, reflects that at a meeting among high-level VRS leaders on 22 September 1995, Milovanovic reported that a team from the Serbian DB, including Filipovic and Bozovic, had arrived and three brigades from the Serbian DB were promised. Milovanovic's testimony at transcript page 15524 is clear that Bozovic and Filipovic were already in the area prior to the SDG's murders. Bozovic and Filipovic were JATD members who were direct subordinates to both accused and paid by the JATD in September and October 1995 as indicated on slide 101. On slide 102 is P2544, which reflects that on 29 September 1995, in a meeting with Mladic, Karadzic stated: "Jovica Stanisic is angry about something. He gave 300 of his men, and the US is begrudging us for having advertised Arkan." This reveals that (a) Stanisic was responsible for sending personnel into the Sanski Most area; (b) Stanisic was abreast of Arkan's role; and (c) he communicated with Karadzic about these issues. This meeting between Karadzic and Mladic took place only six days after Mladic sent Karadzic a dispatch stating that Arkan had identified himself as a member of the MUP of Serbia and RS. And that's P289. Slide 103 shows that the next day Mladic met with Stanisic and Perisic. Stanisic's report reveals that he was well informed about the situation on the ground in Sanski Most and well informed about Arkan's activities. Stanisic stated "We sent 400 people." Stanisic interprets that comment as referring to public security PJP units, citing to Witness Grekulovic's testimony at transcript page 15308 that the chief of the DB could be involved in deploying public security units. Although there is no evidence that Stanisic was referring to public security units in this entry, if the Defence is correct, this would be another element of Stanisic's involvement in the operation on top of supplying and funding JATD and SDG units. On 3 October 1995 Mladic's notebook reflects a meeting with Filipovic and Bozovic as indicated on slide 104. Filipovic reported on Arkan's activities, revealing that as a subordinate of the accused, he was well informed about Arkan. Bozovic reported that, "It was agreed that we would replace the RS police." This again reveals the co-operation among JCE organs in the Sanski Most operations and alludes to units supplied by the accused. In addition to the evidence in the Mladic notebooks, Stanisic and Simatovic demonstrated their authority over the SDG in Sanski Most by paying them. The JATD payment list reveal that as during Operation Pauk, the Serbian DB made payments to the SDG through the end of 1995. Seeking to undercut this powerful evidence against him, Stanisic has presented a number of unsupported theories regarding the per diems. He asserts the possibility that public funds were embezzled, then later asserts that someone in the DB was doing the SDG a favour. The reality is that SDG members known to be in the Sanski Most operations received payments in September and October 1995 as indicated on slide 106. The Prosecution requests that that slide not be broadcast to the public. The per diems are supported by the evidence that the largest amount the DB ever paid to the SDG was received after the Sanski Most operations in September 1995 as indicated on the confidential evidence table, items D31 and 32. Attempting to distance himself from the payment lists, Stanisic argues: "Logic and the DB's financial processing dictates that Stanisic would not have known who were being paid per diems. This is true even if Simatovic paid the per diems himself as the Prosecution suggests." Simatovic, on the other happened, asserts regarding Pauk that he "played no role and had no influence on the disbursement of wages" and "the financial arrangement had been made by Jovica Stanisic." It should be fairly obvious that the Prosecution's case is not that Stanisic would have known by name every individual on the payment lists. Rather, that as chief of the DB, he was the one who set the policy and made the decision about who should be paid, particularly among reserve units and people who were not officially employed by the service. Vujovic, a DB employee and Defence witness, testified that there were some individuals who on their own initiative engaged in amateur surveillance work in Ilok and that at some point the 8th Administration regularised and began to pay them. When asked whether this decision would have to have been approved by the chief of the DB, Vujovic responded, "Of course. Of course, yes." Further, Stanisic's personal exchanges with many unit members at the Kula ceremony including Bozovic reveals that he was personally acquainted with individuals who appeared on per diems. The video of the Kula ceremony also captures the fact that Stanisic began speaking extemporaneously after giving out awards, thus displaying his personal knowledge about the unit. I will play a portion of this speech now, and the translation is on slide 107, so Stanisic's words do not need to be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] There, Frenki's correcting our protocol. We have now actually given out the greatest, the highest awards that can be earned in work of this kind and these are the awards for valor. Each of you that receive this award, be it Opacic in the Knin area or Djurica in the Banija area, and even the story of us as men who tried to help their people. Each one of them is the same, particularly the way it came about, but in essence it speaks of the heroism of our people and what we have put into our unit /inaudible passage/ and who will carry on the tradition of this unit." Stanisic gave this speech after Milosevic left the ceremony. This fact alone rebuts the accused's arguments that they were merely putting on a show for Milosevic and that their discussion of the unit was exaggerated. In light of the totality of the evidence, there is no escaping that the accused funded and remained well informed about the SDG's operations in Sanski Most and supplied JATD units to assist in the same operations. With this pattern of involvement, there can be no reasonable doubt of the accused's liability for the SDG's crimes in Sanski Most where they were acting as tools of Arkan and of both accused to further the common criminal purpose. This concludes my submissions, and I will turn the floor over to Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have now set forth our case. These remarks in conjunction with our written submissions establish a comprehensive and compelling case establishing the crimes charged in the indictment and the accused's responsibility for them. I want to spend a few of these last remaining moments on the issue of a possible sentence. Both of the accused put forward their role in the hostage crisis as meriting mitigation. The Prosecution accepts and recognises that their role in this event may be appropriately considered by the Chamber should it find them guilty of crimes. It is important to recognise when doing so that their involvement in the crimes charged in this indictment continued throughout and after this period. Their participation in the crimes in Sanski Most through Arkan and in Trnovo through the Skorpions both took place around the time of the hostage crisis. Their efforts to free the UN personnel held hostage by the VRS was not a watershed withdrawal from the JCE but an effort to mitigate a situation which the JCE perceived had the potential to ultimately damage their goals. Having said this, the Prosecution does recognise that both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic personally entered Bosnia and Herzegovina during a very dangerous period. The likelihood of additional air-strikes by NATO was real. The likelihood that some members of the VRS would physically resist handing over the hostages was real. The Prosecution recognises that both men willingly assumed dangers to their personal safety and brought over 300 UN personnel to safety. The Prosecution notes that the fact that the accused were able to enter Bosnia during such a volatile period and secure the release of the hostages corroborates the other evidence in this case and demonstrates once again the positions of significant influence they yielded. The Stanisic Defence puts forward Mr. Stanisic's health and advanced age. The Prosecution recognises that he did for the most part co-operate with respect to health issues as they impacted the trial, something which allowed the trial to make regular progress, but this trial did not cause or aggravate his illnesses. They are chronic conditions that he would deal with irrespective of the trial. The Prosecution does accept that Mr. Stanisic played a positive role in the Dayton Peace Accords. He helped unify a fractious delegation and facilitated the ultimate acceptance of the plan by the Bosnian Serbs. One of the most significant factors for a Chamber to consider in assessing an appropriate sentence is the gravity of the offences an accused is convicted of. This is a two-part consideration by a Trial Chamber of both the seriousness of the underlying crimes and the form and degree of an accused's participation. Should the Chamber find the two accused guilty of all of the crimes on the indictment, it would be difficult to imagine crimes of greater severity. The crimes charged in the indictment involve thousands of victims directly impacted by the crimes, crimes which have lasting consequences to this day, crimes that will continue to impact lives long after this Chamber enters its judgement. The last witness in the Prosecution's case in chief was the son of one of the men whose murder by the Skorpions was recorded on video. He recounted for you the day when the television news played as he sat in a cafe in a country far from the former Yugoslavia. As he watched the tape, he had a sense that the man in the video was his father, the man begging his captors for water, a sense that was confirmed shortly afterward. He watched his very own father being murdered by the Skorpions. Since that day, every time he sees something as common place as a glass of water, he is reminded of his father's suffering, his mother's loneliness, his own suffering growing up without his father. Your Honours, this is but one example of the suffering of many who struggle through their lives deeply and daily impacted by the crimes of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic. Should this Chamber come to the conclusion that the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt the accused's criminal responsibility, then they must accept responsibility for the gravity of those crimes. They must be held to account for the great suffering they occasioned. It is for that reason that despite the existence of mitigating factors that I now ask, on behalf of the Prosecutor, Mr. Brammertz that the Chamber impose a sentence of life incarceration should the Chamber find them guilty of these crimes. Before I conclude the Prosecution recognises the many witnesses who appeared to give their evidence during this trial. For the victims it was often a difficult experience to recount what happened to them. A large number of the witnesses were of Serb ethnicity who were either present in the areas where the crimes were committed or were members of the special units of the Serbian DB. They have appeared before this Tribunal because of the strength of their conviction in the importance of the truth. The Prosecution also recognises the co-operation of the government of Serbia. It provided some of the most relevant documentation when requested to do so and allowed former government officials to give evidence. Judges in its courts facilitated our work and the Ministry of Interior assisted when the security of witnesses was a concern. Serbia has made an important contribution to the truth. It is my hope that the Chamber's judgement be it conviction or acquittal, gives the people of Serbia a deeper understanding of the events that had such a deep impact on that country. Your Honours, that concludes our submissions here today. Thank you for receiving them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I think it would not be a good idea to start the closing arguments by the Defence but, rather, give you time and do it tomorrow, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What will be the sequence? Will it be Stanisic Defence first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we've reserved two and a half hours for each Defence team. Then we adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 30th of January, at 2.15 p.m. in this same Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of January, 2013, at 2.15 p.m.
